items.prose: A can maker needs 3 thousand tonnes of aluminium next year. Fixing the price of $x$ thousand tonnes now costs $C(x) = 2(x - 3)^2 + 5|x|$, in £k: a broker's fee on the size of the deal plus a risk charge on the gap to the 3 thousand tonnes. A negative $x$ fixes a sale.

parts.question: Take $a = -1$, $b = 3$ and $\theta = \tfrac12$. What is the chord gap $\theta C(a) + (1 - \theta)C(b) - C(\theta a + (1 - \theta)b)$? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: $C(-1) = 32 + 5 = 37$ and $C(3) = 15$, so the chord sits at 26 above $x = 1$. The curve there is $C(1) = 8 + 5 = 13$, so the gap is 13.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out $C(-1)$, $C(3)$ and $C(1)$ first, then take chord minus curve.

byKey.abs-dropped: You wrote $5|{-1}|$ as $-5$. The fee is charged on the size of the deal, so $C(-1) = 32 + 5 = 37$.
byKey.reversed: That is curve minus chord. The gap is the chord value 26 minus the curve value 13.

explain.text: The mixed point is $x = \tfrac12(-1) + \tfrac12(3) = 1$. The chord value is $\tfrac12(37 + 15) = 26$ and the curve value is 13, a gap of 13. A positive gap is what convexity needs, but it is one pair of points only.

parts.question: Part 1 found a chord gap of 13 for one pair of points. Which argument proves that $C$ is convex on all of $\mathbb{R}$?

options.text: Each term is convex, and so is any nonnegative sum of them.

options.why: $C$ has a corner at 0, where $C''$ does not exist. The second-derivative test needs a second derivative at every point.

options.text: The chord gap in part 1 is positive.
options.why: One chord checks one pair of points and one $\theta$. Convexity asks for every pair and every $\theta$.

options.text: On each side of 0, $C$ is a quadratic plus a line.
options.why: Each piece is convex, but two convex pieces glued at a point can still meet in a dent. The sum rule is what settles it.

feedback.correct: $(x - 3)^2$ and $|x|$ are both convex, and the weights 2 and 5 are positive. So $C$ is convex, corner and all.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look for a rule that needs no derivative at $x = 0$.

explain.text: $(x - 3)^2$ has second derivative 2. For $|x|$ the triangle inequality gives $|\theta a + (1 - \theta)b| \le \theta|a| + (1 - \theta)|b|$, which is the chord inequality. The weights 2 and 5 are positive, so the sum is convex with no derivative needed at 0.

parts.question: Part 2 showed that $C$ is convex, so a point with $C'(x) = 0$ is its global minimum. For $x > 0$ the cost is $C(x) = 2(x - 3)^2 + 5x$. Where is $C'(x) = 0$? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: $C'(x) = 4(x - 3) + 5 = 0$ gives $x = 1.75$. It is positive, so it lies on the piece we differentiated.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Differentiate $2(x - 3)^2 + 5x$ term by term and set the result to 0.

byKey.no-fee: 3 is the tonnage needed, the best deal if there were no fee. The fee's slope of 5 pulls the best deal below 3.
byKey.fee-sign: You subtracted the fee's slope. For $x > 0$ the fee $5x$ rises with $x$, so $C'(x) = 4(x - 3) + 5$.

explain.text: On $x > 0$, $C'(x) = 4(x - 3) + 5$, which is zero at $x = 1.75$. That point is inside $x > 0$, so it is a local minimum of $C$. $C$ is convex, so it is the global minimum.

parts.question: Using the minimiser $x = 1.75$ from part 3, what is the smallest cost, in £k? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $x = 1.75$ into both terms of $C$.

byKey.half: You dropped the 2 in front of the square: $2 \times 1.5625 = 3.125$, not 1.5625.
byKey.no-fee: That is the risk charge alone. Add the fee, $5 \times 1.75 = 8.75$.

explain.text: $C(1.75) = 3.125 + 8.75 = 11.875$. It beats fixing nothing, $C(0) = 18$, and fixing all 3 thousand tonnes, $C(3) = 15$.

parts.question: A credit limit now caps the deal at $x \le 1.2$. Using what parts 2 to 4 showed about $C$, what is the least cost with $x \le 1.2$? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $C$ is still falling at the limit: $C'(1.2) = -7.2 + 5 = -2.2$. So the best allowed deal is $x = 1.2$, with $C(1.2) = 6.48 + 6 = 12.48$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask whether $C$ is still falling when $x$ reaches 1.2.

byKey.unconstrained: That needs $x = 1.75$, which breaks the new limit. On $x \le 1.2$ the cost is lowest at the edge.
byKey.at-zero: 0 is the corner of $C$, but $C(0) = 18$. The cost keeps falling from 0 all the way to the limit.
byKey.fee-dropped: That is the risk charge only. Add the fee, $5 \times 1.2 = 6$.

explain.text: The allowed set $x \le 1.2$ is convex and $C$ is convex, so a local minimum there is global. $C' < 0$ on $(0, 1.2]$, so the minimum is at the edge, where $C' \ne 0$. The limit costs $12.48 - 11.875 = 0.605$, about £600.

items.prose: A broker buys advertising to win new accounts. Spending $x$ on search ads and $y$ on podcasts, in £k with $x, y \ge 0$, brings in $N(x, y) = 6\sqrt{x} + 3\sqrt{y}$ hundred accounts. The broker wants at least 30 hundred accounts, $N(x, y) \ge 30$, for the least total spend $x + y$.

parts.question: What is the second derivative of $6\sqrt{x}$ for $x > 0$?

feedback.correct: $6\sqrt{x} = 6x^{1/2}$ has first derivative $3x^{-1/2}$. Once more gives $-\tfrac32x^{-3/2}$, which is negative for every $x > 0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Write $6\sqrt{x}$ as $6x^{1/2}$ and use the power rule twice.

byKey.sign: The power rule brings down $-\tfrac12$ the second time, so the result is negative: $-\tfrac32x^{-3/2}$.
byKey.first: That is the first derivative. Differentiate $3x^{-1/2}$ once more.
byKey.power: Lower the power as well as multiplying by it: $3x^{-1/2}$ becomes $-\tfrac32x^{-3/2}$.

explain.text: The second derivative $-\tfrac32x^{-3/2}$ is negative, so $6\sqrt{x}$ is concave and $-6\sqrt{x}$ is convex. The same holds for $3\sqrt{y}$. Each extra £k on one channel brings fewer accounts than the last.

parts.question: Using the sign found in part 1, which argument shows that the plans with $N(x, y) \ge 30$ form a convex set?

options.text: $30 - 6\sqrt{x} - 3\sqrt{y}$ is a sum of convex functions, and the plans are where it is at most 0.
$N$ is convex, and the set where a convex function is at least 30 is convex.
options.why: Part 1 makes $N$ concave, not convex. It is $-N$ that is convex, and the plans are where $-N \le -30$.

options.text: $N$ rises in both $x$ and $y$, so more spend never leaves the set.
options.why: Rising is not enough. $\max(x, y) \ge 1$ rises in both, yet $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ pass and their midpoint fails.

options.text: Every at-least limit, whatever its function, gives a convex set.
options.why: $x^2 \ge 1$ is an at-least limit, and it leaves out the gap between $-1$ and 1.

feedback.correct: Part 1 makes $-6\sqrt{x}$ and $-3\sqrt{y}$ convex, and adding the constant 30 keeps that. Points where a convex function is no more than 0 form a convex set.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Move everything to one side so that the limit reads $f(x, y) \le 0$, then ask whether $f$ is convex.

explain.text: $N \ge 30$ is the same as $f(x, y) = 30 - 6\sqrt{x} - 3\sqrt{y} \le 0$. By part 1, $f$ is a constant plus two convex functions, so it is convex. Its sublevel set at 0 is convex, and with a linear spend the whole problem is convex.

parts.question: Part 2 showed that the problem is convex. Put $u = \sqrt{x}$ and $v = \sqrt{y}$. The spend becomes $u^2 + v^2$ and the limit the half-plane $6u + 3v \ge 30$. Spend rises with $u$ and $v$, so the cheapest plan meets the limit exactly: $v = 10 - 2u$. How much does that plan spend on search ads, $x$, in £k? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: Along the line the spend is $u^2 + (10 - 2u)^2$, with slope $2u - 4(10 - 2u) = 10u - 40$. It is 0 at $u = 4$, so $x = u^2 = 16$ and $v = 2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Substitute $v = 10 - 2u$ into $u^2 + v^2$, set the slope in $u$ to 0, then square $u$.

byKey.gave-u: 4 is $u = \sqrt{x}$. The spend on search is $u^2 = 16$.
byKey.corner: 25 buys the whole target on search ads alone. Splitting it does better: £16k on search and £4k on podcasts.
byKey.no-chain: The slope of $(10 - 2u)^2$ is $-4(10 - 2u)$: the chain rule adds the factor $-2$. Then $10u = 40$ and $u = 4$.

explain.text: In $(u, v)$ the spend is a bowl and the limit a half-plane: a convex problem again. Along the line the spend is a convex parabola in $u$, so $u = 4$ is its global minimum. Back in pounds, $x = 16$ and $y = 4$.

parts.question: Using $x = 16$ from part 3, what is the least total spend, in £k? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: $v = 10 - 2 \times 4 = 2$, so $y = 4$ and the spend is $16 + 4 = 20$: £20k. Check: $N = 6 \times 4 + 3 \times 2 = 30$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find $v$ from $v = 10 - 2u$, square it for $y$, and add $x$.

byKey.search-only: 16 is the search budget alone. Podcasts take $y = v^2 = 4$ more.
byKey.roots: 6 is $u + v$, in square-root units. The spend is $u^2 + v^2 = 16 + 4$.
byKey.corner: 25 is the cost of reaching 30 hundred on search ads alone. The split plan saves £5k.

explain.text: The cheapest plan spends £16k on search and £4k on podcasts. The problem is convex, so no other plan reaches 30 hundred accounts for less than £20k.

parts.question: The board may change the target. Repeat the steps of parts 3 and 4 with a target of $T$ hundred accounts in place of 30. Write the least spend, in £k, as an expression in $T$.

feedback.correct: The line is now $v = \tfrac{T}{3} - 2u$, and the slope $10u - \tfrac{4T}{3}$ is 0 at $u = \tfrac{2T}{15}$. Then $v = \tfrac{T}{15}$ and the spend is $\tfrac{4T^2 + T^2}{225} = \tfrac{T^2}{45}$, which gives 20 at $T = 30$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Write the limit as $6u + 3v = T$, solve for $v$, and minimise $u^2 + v^2$ in $u$ as in part 3.

byKey.linear: That scales the £20k in proportion to the target. Both $u$ and $v$ grow in proportion to $T$, so the spend grows with $T^2$.
byKey.search-only: That buys the whole target on search ads, $x = (\tfrac{T}{6})^2$. The split plan is cheaper for every $T > 0$.
byKey.podcast-only: That buys the whole target on podcasts, $y = (\tfrac{T}{3})^2$, the dearest way.

explain.text: The least spend is $\tfrac{T^2}{45}$, a convex function of the target. Doubling the target to 60 hundred accounts quadruples the spend, to £80k.

items.prose: An energy firm owns a power plant whose yearly earnings $P$ move with fuel markets. It sells $a$ units of a gas forward $F_1$ and $b$ of a carbon forward $F_2$; a negative amount is a purchase. With $\operatorname{Var}(F_1) = 1$, $\operatorname{Cov}(F_1, F_2) = 3$, $\operatorname{Var}(F_2) = 10$, $\operatorname{Cov}(P, F_1) = \operatorname{Cov}(P, F_2) = 1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(P) = 6$, what is left, $P - aF_1 - bF_2$, has variance $V(a, b) = a^2 + 6ab + 10b^2 - 2a - 2b + 6$.

parts.question: What is the determinant of the Hessian of $V$? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the three second partial derivatives of $V$ first.

byKey.half-cross: The mixed partial of $6ab$ is 6, not 3. With 6 off the diagonal, $\det\mathbf{H} = 40 - 36 = 4$.
byKey.no-two: That is $1 \times 10 - 3^2$, from the forwards' covariance matrix. Each second derivative of $V$ is double the matching entry, so the determinant is $4 \times 1 = 4$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{H} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 6\\ 6 & 20\end{pmatrix}$, twice the covariance matrix of $(F_1, F_2)$. Its determinant is $40 - 36 = 4$.

parts.question: Using $\det\mathbf{H} = 4$ from part 1, what follows about $V$?

options.text: $V$ is strictly convex: the eigenvalues multiply to 4 and add to 22, so both are positive.
$V$ is convex because $V_{aa}$ and $V_{bb}$ are positive; the determinant is not needed.
options.why: Positive diagonal entries are not enough. With $7ab$ in place of $6ab$ they are still 2 and 20, yet the determinant is $40 - 49 = -9$ and $V$ is a saddle.

options.text: $V$ is strictly convex because the determinant is positive; the trace plays no part.
options.why: Two negative eigenvalues also multiply to a positive number, as for $-V$. The positive trace rules that out.

options.text: $V$ is not convex, because 4 is small next to the diagonal entries.
options.why: A small determinant means one small eigenvalue, about 0.18, not a negative one. The bowl is shallow in one direction but still a bowl.

feedback.correct: $\lambda_1\lambda_2 = 4 > 0$ and $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 22 > 0$, so both eigenvalues are positive and $\mathbf{H}$ is positive definite.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the product and the sum of the two eigenvalues.

explain.text: For a 2 by 2 matrix, the determinant is the eigenvalues' product and the trace their sum. A product of 4 and a sum of 22 force both to be positive, about 0.18 and 21.82. So $V$ is strictly convex and has at most one minimiser.

parts.question: Using the strict convexity from part 2, solve $\nabla V = \mathbf{0}$. How many units $a$ of $F_1$ does the firm sell? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: $2a + 6b = 2$ and $6a + 20b = 2$. The first gives $a = 1 - 3b$, then $6 + 2b = 2$, so $b = -2$ and $a = 7$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Write $V_a = 0$ and $V_b = 0$, then eliminate $a$.

byKey.sign: Check the sign of $b$: $6(1 - 3b) + 20b = 2$ gives $2b = -4$, so $b = -2$ and $a = 1 + 6 = 7$.

explain.text: Both partial derivatives vanish at $(a, b) = (7, -2)$, and by part 2 no other point does as well. The firm sells 7 units of $F_1$ and buys 2 of $F_2$.

parts.question: Using $(a, b) = (7, -2)$ from part 3, what is the smallest variance left? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $a = 7$ and $b = -2$ into every term of $V$.

byKey.unhedged: 6 is $V(0, 0)$, the variance with no forwards. The best pair brings it down to 1.
byKey.no-constant: You left out $\operatorname{Var}(P) = 6$. The variance left is $-5 + 6 = 1$.

explain.text: Substituting gives $V = 1$. The forwards remove five sixths of the variance, and the best pair buys 2 units of $F_2$.

parts.question: The firm may not buy carbon forwards, so now $b \ge 0$. The pair from part 3 breaks this. What is the smallest variance left with $b \ge 0$? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: On the edge $b = 0$, $V = a^2 - 2a + 6$ is lowest at $a = 1$, with $V = 5$. There $V_b = 6 - 2 = 4 > 0$, so moving into $b > 0$ only raises $V$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The free minimum is outside the allowed set, so look along its edge.

byKey.free: 1 needs $b = -2$, a purchase of $F_2$. The ban moves the best pair to the edge $b = 0$.
byKey.clip: That keeps $a = 7$ and sets $b = 0$. Re-solve along the edge: $a = 1$ gives 5.

explain.text: The set $b \ge 0$ is a half-plane, so it is convex, and $V$ is convex, so a local minimum there is global. An interior minimum would be a free one, and the only free one has $b = -2$, so the answer lies on $b = 0$. There the least variance is 5, so the ban costs 4.
